title: Vance Launches H-1B Fraud Crackdown With Dozens of DOL Subpoenas
excerpt: The Trump administration expands its anti-fraud campaign to employment visas, with the Labor Department targeting employers and foreign entities accused of exploiting the H-1B programme.
body:
• Vice President JD Vance announced a sweeping H-1B visa fraud investigation at an anti-fraud event in Milwaukee, with the Department of Labor issuing dozens of subpoenas.
  • The DOL Inspector General has uncovered schemes involving fraudulent applications, coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and below-wage labor flooding the market.
  • Department of Homeland Security assessments found up to 21% of H-1B petitions were fraudulent, with some tied to forced-labor networks.
  • Indian nationals account for approximately 73% of H-1B visa recipients, making the crackdown a significant concern for the diaspora community.

Vice President JD Vance has launched a fresh offensive against alleged fraud in the H-1B visa programme, announcing that the Department of Labor has fired off dozens of subpoenas as part of a sweeping investigation into employers and foreign entities accused of exploiting the system.

Speaking at an anti-fraud event in Milwaukee, Vance framed the enforcement action as central to the Trump administration's broader effort to protect American workers. "American jobs ought to go to American workers and not foreign fraudsters, and the Department of Labor is fighting back against it," he said.

A Broader Anti-Fraud Campaign

The investigation extends the administration's anti-fraud task force beyond federal spending programmes to include employment-based visas. Vance described the H-1B programme as originally designed for "a brilliant technology person or a brilliant scientist or a brilliant doctor" but said large corporations and overseas entities were misusing it to suppress American wages.

"Big corporations and fraudsters overseas are using this programme to undercut the wages of American workers. We're saying no more."

— JD Vance, Vice President

Department of Labor Inspector General Anthony D'Esposito told the New York Post that the probe has already uncovered "widespread schemes in which employers and labor brokers submitted fraudulent applications, exploited foreign workers through coercive wage-kickback arrangements, and undercut American workers by flooding the market with below-wage labor."

Scale of the Problem

The scope of fraud appears substantial. Department of Homeland Security assessments have found that as much as 21% of H-1B petitions were fraudulent. D'Esposito said the schemes had been used to bilk the medical industry to the tune of "hundreds of millions" of dollars, with some operations run by forced-labor networks and human traffickers.

The investigation will target not only H-1B visa holders but also employment-based green card recipients. "This is not just people working in factories or actual labor," D'Esposito said. "These are people working in medical facilities and doctors' offices that are actually putting people in harm's way."

Impact on Indian Professionals

The crackdown carries outsized implications for Indian professionals in the United States. According to the Pew Research Center, approximately 73% of H-1B recipients come from India, with the majority holding master's degrees and working in technology, engineering, healthcare, and finance.

The H-1B programme caps annual visas at 65,000 for most private employers, with an additional 20,000 slots for candidates with advanced degrees from U.S. institutions. According to immigration advocacy group FWD.us, around 730,000 H-1B visa holders currently live in the United States, along with nearly 550,000 dependents.

The Trump administration has already introduced a $100,000 one-time fee for new H-1B applicants, a move challenged by 20 states — all led by Democrats. Immigration lawyers have pushed back on the fraud characterisation, with Kelly Fortier, a partner at Michael Best who has worked with H-1B cases for over 20 years, telling the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel: "I personally have not seen it in my day-to-day practice."

What's Next

Major technology companies including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, and Apple are among the largest employers of H-1B visa holders, making the investigation's outcome a bellwether for the tech industry's ability to recruit global talent. With more than half of H-1B holders possessing master's degrees and working in specialised fields, immigration advocates warn that the crackdown risks conflating legitimate skilled immigration with genuine fraud cases.

For the roughly 730,000 Indian H-1B holders and their families in the United States, the investigation adds another layer of uncertainty to an already turbulent immigration landscape under the Trump administration.
